newsitem.title: SWEDEN: TENNIS-NEW GENERATION PICKS UP SWEDISH TENNIS TORCH.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-NEW GENERATION PICKS UP SWEDISH TENNIS TORCH.

text.p: A new generation of tennis players led by Thomas Enqvist and dubbed the Wild Gang have stepped into the tennis shoes of celebrated Swedes Stefan Edberg and Bjorn Borg.

As the 30-year-old Edberg said goodbye to the international circuit at the Stockholm Open on Sunday, Enqvist, 22, was named the country's new tennis king, after ending 1996 with two tour victories in a row.
"King Edberg has abdicated. The crown prince is called Thomas Enqvist," proclaimed the Swedish tabloid Expressen.
Edberg donned the mantle of the man who launched Sweden as a tennis nation, Bjorn Borg. Borg won Wimbledon a record five times running during his heyday in the 1970s and early 1980s.
Edberg was listed among the world's top 10 players for 10 years, winning six Grand Slam titles before announcing his retirement this year.
"Stefan has been a terrific ambassador for Sweden and for sport," said ATP executive Larry Scott in a ceremony to bid Edberg farewell at Stockholm's Royal Tennis Hall.
The ATP has decided to name its Sportsman of the Year award after the cool-tempered Edberg in recognition of his sportsmanship and respect among the international tennis fraternity.
As Edberg departed, Enqvist moved out of his shadow.
After five years on the circuit, Enqvist has risen to number eight in the ATP rankings, and is seen as the leader of the a new generation.
He is ending 1996 on a high note, retaining his Stockholm Open title on Sunday with a straight sets victory over American Todd Martin one week after taking the Paris Open title.
The two wins have earned him the reserve place at the lucrative ATP Tour World Championship starting in Hanover on November 19. He was an unheralded semifinalist there last year.
But it is not just Enqvist who carries Sweden's tennis hopes. Swedes dominated this year's Stockholm Open.
The big-serving Nicklas Kulti, 25, knocked Edberg out of the tournament in the first round before he fell victim to compatriot, 23-year-old Patrik Fredriksson.
But the depth of the Swedish squad was really revealed in the semifinals on Saturday when three out of the four slots were taken by the new generation.
Although Fredriksson was defeated by Enqvist in the quarter-finals, 21-year-old Thomas Johansson and 20-year-old Magnus Norman, made it through to the semifinals.
"The wild gang," was the nickname coined by the tabloid Aftonbladet to describe the new breed of young happy-go-lucky players, who entered the Stockholm Open with wild cards and upset the seedings.
American Todd Martin, beaten by Enqvist in the Stockholm Open final, said he was impressed by the new Swedish players.
"I was extremely impressed by Fredriksson when he knocked out Kulti and I have a feeling that we will see a lot more of these guys on the tour," Martin said.
